name: LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference
problem: KV cache grows far past GPU memory in real deployments, and moving it to CPU/DRAM/SSD with existing ad-hoc paths is slow, so cache reuse across queries and across engines is impractical.
mechanism: A dedicated KV cache layer between the engine and storage with an explicit connector interface, non-blocking save/load paths that overlap transfer with compute, and a store-back policy that decides what is worth persisting. The design goal is reuse ACROSS queries and ACROSS engines, not just offload.
speedup_reported: The paper's own motivation is real-world usage statistics showing total stored KV cache growing far beyond GPU capacity; it claims to be 'the first and so far the most efficient open-source' KV cache layer. NO specific speedup multiple is stated in the abstract, so no multiple is recorded here rather than inventing one. Any TTFT reduction figure must be read from the paper's evaluation section together with its cache hit-rate assumption — on a cold workload with zero hits there is no gain by construction.

THE DECISIVE ARGUMENT. The arXiv API returns published 2025-10-08 for 2510.09665 (v2 2025-12-05). ICLR 2025
author notifications were January 2025 and its conference April 2025; the next ICLR cycle open after this
preprint appeared is ICLR 2026. A paper first posted to arXiv in OCTOBER 2025 therefore CANNOT have been an
ICLR 2025 paper - the decision preceded the preprint by roughly nine months. This is stronger than a negative
index search because it does not depend on any index being complete: it is a consistency argument between two
independently documented dates. Source w6p-arxiv-api-lmcache-timing.

THE SEARCH REPRODUCES TOO, on a different endpoint. OpenReview api2 for 'LMCache' (source
w6p-openreview-api2-lmcache-only-corr) returns exactly one titled, venued record for this paper: forum
M1BI86jGg6, venue 'CoRR 2025', venueid 'dblp.org/journals/CORR/2025' - the arXiv deposit reflected back, since a
dblp.org/journals/CORR venueid is the class that means 'no proceedings entry'. The other titled hits in the

anywhere. This independently confirms wave 4's finding rather than contradicting it.

HOW THE ERROR GOT IN, since 'the search said so' is not good enough. This record's OWN source record
pap-sys-lmcache-openreview states 'content.venue = ICLR 2025 Poster' and its url is not a forum page but an
api2 SEARCH query - a claim of an exact venue string with no forum id behind it, against a search that returns
something different today. pap-sys-lmcache-arxiv repeats the same sentence. A search URL is not a citation: it
cannot be re-read to confirm what it said at the time it was read, which is exactly why this claim was able to
sit in the repo marked 'verified' and then survive a wave that could not reproduce it. Both source notes are
left in place UNCHANGED on the record that cites them - they are the provenance of the error, and rewriting
them would destroy the evidence for how it happened. What is corrected is the paper record.

WHAT IS NOT CHANGED: adoption=in-upstream-engine stands on independent grounds and is unaffected by the venue.
vLLM ships LMCacheConnectorV1 and LMCacheMPConnector as documented connectors, including for disaggregated
prefill, and the LMCache repository is actively pushed. Being an in-upstream-engine CONNECTOR is different from
being a vLLM subsystem - vLLM's own KV management is not LMCache. arxiv_id unchanged (2510.09665).

THE ABSTRACT FIGURE THIS RECORD NOW OWES ITS READERS, since the venue correction raises rather than lowers
confidence and the headline number deserves to be stated: LMCACHE reports UP TO 15x throughput improvement
when combined with vLLM, on multi-round question answering and document analysis. That is a
with-LMCache-against-without-LMCache comparison on a prefix-reuse-heavy workload, so it is bounded by the cache
hit rate by construction - on a cold single-turn workload with zero prefix hits there is no gain at all. The
paper's own operational finding is the more useful one for a deployment reader: context truncation, widely
applied in industry, roughly HALVES the prefix cache hit ratio. That is a real operational consequence of a
widely-applied optimisation and is worth more than the 15x.
